t: How To Send Students To Time-Out
q: Time-out should take place at a desk separated from classmates. It’s best to have one or two strictly for this purpose.
Only send students to time-out if their behavior triggers such a consequence (as is stated in your classroom management plan). Time-out should never be a choice you make.
But be quick and direct. And never add a lecture, a scolding, or your two cents worth. Let time-out be the only consequence.
Don’t escort students to time-out. Simply inform them and then move on with whatever you were doing. Time-out should never be an interruption.
Students placed in time-out are no longer part of the class, and they need to feel excluded. Not as a punishment per se, but as a message that anyone who interferes with learning is not welcome.
When a student in time-out decides they’re ready to follow rules and be part of the class again, they must raise their hand and wait for you.
When a student is ready to return from time-out, welcome them back. A simple “Good to have you back” will do. Never hold a grudge, give a cold shoulder, or be short with them.

t: How To Be A Classroom Management Rock Star https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/12/11/how-to-be-a-classroom-management-rock-star/
q: To create the classroom you really want, you need a clear vision of what it looks like. Otherwise, you’ll be a rudderless ship, bounced around by the tides of circumstance and never getting where you want to go.
The clearer your vision, and the more vivid it appears in the mind, the sooner it will come true.
Getting through tough times to become a classroom management rock star takes an unshakeable belief in yourself.

As soon as you shutter away the justifications, excuses, and 101 reasons why your students can’t behave, and take responsibility for the behavior that takes place on your watch, you’ll finally—blissfully—be empowered to create the class you really want.
When you make your happiness a priority, when you decide to accept nothing less than awesomeness for yourself and your classroom, then that’s exactly what you’ll get.
Don’t be like that coulda-shoulda-woulda rock star, playing the local clubs, semi-satisfied, never rising to meet his potential.
Why not go after what you really want? Why not create a classroom you can’t wait to get to every morning?

t: 8 Things Teachers Do To Encourage Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/12/04/8-things-teachers-do-to-encourage-misbehavior/
q: The only classroom management-related problems that don’t have solutions are those we’re unaware of. Once illuminated, there is always a way to solve the problem or make it manageable.
Talking over students breeds inattentiveness, side-talking, and poor listening.
Being in a hurry creates tension in the classroom, causing restlessness, excitability, and poor behavior.
Answering students who don’t raise their hand encourages disrespect and communicates to your students that your classroom management plan is no longer valid.
Negative thoughts about students always bubble to the surface-body language, tone of voice, sarcasm-causing resentment, misbehavior and, ultimately, revenge.
